item.title: Greet ziet haar grootste verrassing bijna over het hoofd Winnaarsverhalen 16 september 2026 Gouden enveloppen vallen natuurlijk meteen op. Een gloednieuwe BMW blijkbaar iets minder. Lees meer
item.description:
Gouden enveloppen vallen natuurlijk meteen op. Een gloednieuwe BMW blijkbaar iets minder. Op postcode 9351 DA in Leek verrast Gaston de winnaars met de PostcodeStraatprijs. En Greet? Die moet nog even goed om zich heen kijken om haar extra verrassing te ontdekken.

woensdag 16 september 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

 Zo vader, zo dochter

Jan en Antje genieten van het mooie weer in hun tuin als Gaston langskomt. Als ze horen dat ze € 25.000,- winnen, kan Antje het bijna niet geloven. "Wauw, net als mijn vader! Hij won in 2009 ook de PostcodeStraatprijs."Het stel weet al wat ze met het geld willen doen. Het huis krijgt een opfrisbeurt met nieuw behang en een lik verf. 

Nog maar een weekje weg? 

Bij Douwe en Debbie staat de auto nog vol vakantiebagage voor de deur. Ze komen net terug van een week op Ameland. Maar na het zien van de cheque van € 25.000,- begint het alweer te kriebelen. "Ik denk dat we nog een week vakantie gaan boeken. Misschien dit keer wel naar een ander Waddeneiland." 

Mensen helpen

Hosein ontvangt een cheque van € 25.000,-. Hij hoeft niet lang na te denken over de bestemming van zijn prijs. "Ik wil mensen helpen", zegt hij resoluut. Op de vraag van Gaston hoe hij dat wil doen, antwoordt hij: "Ik kom uit Iran. Daar wil ik de mensen helpen die te maken hebben met de oorlog." 

Waar staat de auto dan? 

Greet is heel blij met haar € 25.000,-, al weet ze nog niet wat ze ermee gaat doen. Dan blijkt Gaston nóg iets voor haar te hebben. Hij haalt de sleutels van een gloednieuwe BMW tevoorschijn. Ze zag de auto eerst even niet staan, maar na het omdraaien schrikt ze lachend. Ze is heel erg blij!

item.title: Nog nooit gebeurd: Joey wint 3 keer bij Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht Winnaarsverhalen 16 september 2026 Dit gebeurde nog nooit in de 26-jarige geschiedenis van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht. Lees meer
item.description:
Dit gebeurde nog nooit in de 26-jarige geschiedenis van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht. Joey uit Waddinxveen geeft in de eerste ronde bij 3 van de 5 vragen als snelste het goede antwoord. Daarmee pakt hij een plek achter de desk, wint hij € 10.000,- én een gloednieuwe BMW. En zijn bijzondere avond gaat verder. Joey bereikt ook de finale en wint daar maar liefst € 130.000,-. 

woensdag 16 september 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Meespelen én een koffer kiezen

Het begint al in de eerste ronde, bij de tweede vraag. Joey geeft als snelste het juiste antwoord en verovert een plek achter de desk. Even later is hij wéér de snelste. Dit keer kiest hij voor een koffer. Daarin zit € 10.000,-. 

Nog een koffer te openen

En dan gebeurt het nóg een keer. Bij de laatste vraag reageert Joey opnieuw als snelste. “Dit hebben we echt nog nooit meegemaakt”, zegt Linda de Mol verbaasd. Zijn 3e succes levert hem een gloednieuwe BMW op.

Joey bereikt de finale 

Maar Joey’s avond is nog lang niet voorbij. Hij bereikt de finale en speelt daar voor de grote geldbedragen. Uiteindelijk accepteert hij bij een bod van € 130.000,- voor zekerheid. “Soms moet je accepteren dat het genoeg is.” 
 

Wat gaat Joey doen met zijn prijzen?

€ 130.000,-, € 10.000,- én een nieuwe BMW op één avond. Denise vat het mooi samen: “Het is net alsof we in een droom leven”, zegt Denise, de partner van Joey. Met het geld willen Joey en Denise hun huis verbouwen en mooie reizen maken met hun gezin en familie.

Kijk jij volgende zondag mee?

Tussen 6 september en 18 oktober 2026 geniet je iedere zondag om 19:55 uur van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht op SBS6. Wil je Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht terugkijken? Dat kan via KIJK.nl.

item.title: Foundations Commit $25M to Strengthen Nonprofits’ Access to Insurance
item.description:
Image courtesy of iStock.

The following first appeared in Nonprofits Insurance Alliance. The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily represent the views of the Rockefeller Brothers Fund.

A consortium of prominent foundations collaborates in support of Nonprofits Insurance Alliance and the nonprofit sector it serves.

Nine prominent foundations have joined together to provide $25 million in support of Nonprofits Insurance Alliance (NIA), a nonprofit insurance cooperative that serves more than 25,000 nonprofits across the country.

NIA is a 37-year-old group of nonprofit-governed insurers, built by nonprofits, that exists solely to provide the property and casualty insurance the nonprofit sector needs. NIA is a 501(c)(3) charitable nonprofit itself.

This support recognizes NIA as an essential part of the nonprofit sector’s infrastructure at a time when insurance has become difficult for many organizations to secure and afford and will allow NIA to continue to be a buffer against unpredictable market changes in a period of rapid growth and change.

In recent years, nonprofits have experienced strain due to limited availability of affordable and comprehensive insurance in the commercial market. Insurance is an operating requirement and without it, nonprofits cannot provide critical services in communities across the country. In these market conditions, NIA's services have been especially critical.

“Commercial insurers have a model that benefits from going in and out of markets to bolster profits and shed perceived risk,” said Pamela Davis, Founder, President, and CEO of Nonprofits Insurance Alliance. “That works fine for them, but it does not work for nonprofits and their insurance brokers, who need to scramble when coverage is unexpectedly nonrenewed. Unlike commercial insurers, NIA is dedicated solely to the nonprofit sector.”

The foundations’ support helps to address these insurance market challenges and expands an essential source of insurance for nonprofits, now and into the future. 

“We were pleased to be part of this collaboration in support of an important part of the nonprofit infrastructure,” said Kimberlee Cornett, Director of Impact Investments at the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and a leader of the foundation consortium that provided support. “Access to property and casualty insurance is central to nonprofits’ ability to do their work in communities across the country.”

“The California Endowment is grateful to NIA for its steadfast commitment to supporting nonprofits through various insurance industry cycles over the last several decades,” said Aifuwa Ehigiator, Investments Officer, Program Related Investments. “We were excited to be a part of the foundation group that supported NIA so that they support nonprofits for years to come.”

The nine foundations providing support are the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation, The California Endowment, The Kresge Foundation, the Surdna Foundation, the Soros Economic Development Fund, the Kenneth Rainin Foundation, the California Wellness Foundation, and the Rockefeller Brothers Fund. 

“We are grateful to these visionary foundations for recognizing that insurance access is essential to the nonprofit sector’s ability to serve communities,” Davis said. “Their support helps NIA address nonprofits’ growing need for stable, sector-focused coverage to support their community-based missions.”

Learn more about the Nonprofits Insurance Alliance.

item.title: Från idé till bok: unga författare firades i Sandviken
item.description:
Det märks att det här är en speciell dag.

På scenen i centrala Sandviken står barn och unga som under de senaste två åren arbetat med sina egna berättelser. Framför dem står stolta familjemedlemmar, vänner och nyfikna åskådare. En efter en kliver de fram för att berätta om sina böcker, sina karaktärer och hur deras idéer blev till färdiga berättelser.

När Postkodlotteriets Stiftelse besökte Rapatacs projekt Jag är en författare! blev det tydligt att böckerna bara är en del av resultatet. Minst lika viktigt är det självförtroende som växer när unga får möjlighet att uttrycka sig, bli lyssnade på och känna stolthet över det de skapat.

”Det roligaste var att jag äntligen fick visa mina tankar!”, berättar Ariana, en av författarna.

Från idé till egen bok

Projektet drivs av Rapatac och syftar till att stärka barns och ungas läsförståelse, skrivförmåga, självförtroende och framtidstro genom att låta dem bli författare på riktigt.

Enligt Skolverkets senaste PIRLS-studie har svenska elevers läsförståelse sjunkit sedan 2016, samtidigt som färre barn läser på fritiden. Mot den bakgrunden blir initiativ som Jag är en författare! alltmer aktuellt. Sedan starten av projektet har över hundra barn och unga deltagit i projektets löpande läs- och skrivaktiviteter. Genom workshops, högläsning, poddar, illustration och kreativt skapande har deltagarna utvecklat både sitt språk och tron på sin egen förmåga. Enligt projektets delrapport upplever en stor majoritet av deltagarna att deras läsning och skrivande har förbättrats, samtidigt som självförtroendet stärkts. 

”För oss handlar det också om att väcka nyfikenhet och läslust och om att ge barn möjlighet att se sig själva som någon som kan skapa, berätta och bli lyssnad på. Stödet från Postkodlotteriets Stiftelse har gjort det möjligt för oss att ge fler barn den upplevelsen och att skapa något som blir bestående.” Säger organisationsutvecklaren Matilda Gavlén från Rapatac.

”Jag satte ihop alla mina favoritböcker”

En av dagens mest produktiva författare var Saatthvick, som skrivit två böcker i serien Kristallens magi.

”Jag älskar att läsa! Jag satte ihop alla mina favoritböcker och skrev en egen.”

Att stå framför publiken och berätta om sitt arbete var en särskild upplevelse.

”Det känns otroligt att ha skrivit två böcker! Ge aldrig upp, om ni har ett mål så fortsätt kämpa!” säger Saatthvick med glöd i blicken.

Även Jad Altalli berättade stolt om sin bok Det otäcka godiset.

”Jag ville ta allt som fanns i mitt huvud och lägga det i en bok.” Boken handlar om att ta emot godis från en främmande man och när man åt det så förvandlades man till ett monster.

Flera av deltagarna beskrev hur skrivandet gett dem möjlighet att uttrycka tankar och idéer de länge burit på. Ariana, som skrivit Mellanrummet, sammanfattade känslan:

”Det roligaste var att jag äntligen fick visa mina tankar!”

Ett stöd som gör skillnad

Mathilda Gavlén igen om ungdomarnas stolthet. ”Genom stödet har barn och unga inte bara fått träna på att läsa, skriva och uttrycka sig, utan också upptäcka att deras egna tankar, idéer och berättelser har ett värde. Det skapar en stolthet och ett självförtroende som sträcker sig långt bortom själva skrivandet”.

Varje bok berättar en större historia

Iris Edelstam från Postkodlotteriets Stiftelse, som besökte evenemanget, lyfter fram betydelsen av projektet.

”Det som imponerar mest är inte bara böckerna i sig, utan all den utveckling som ligger bakom dem. Varje bok berättar en större historia om mod, kreativitet och framtidstro. Att se barn och unga stå på scen och presentera sina verk med sådan stolthet är otroligt inspirerande.”

Blickar framåt

Firandet i Sandviken markerade en viktig milstolpe, men också början på något större. Böckerna blir en del av det växande Barnens bibliotek och står som bevis på vad som kan hända när unga får möjlighet att tro på sina idéer och sina berättelser. Böckerna kommer också att finnas tillgängliga att låna på Sandvikens två bibliotek.

Och som en av dagens författare, Daania, lovade från scenen:

”Det kommer fler böcker från mig!”

item.title: Een bijzondere droom komt na 20 jaar alsnog uit Winnaarsverhalen 15 september 2026 Een nieuwe auto, cadeaus voor de kleinkinderen én een droombruiloft in Afrika. In Zoetermeer weten ze wel raad met die gouden enveloppen. Lees meer
item.description:
Een nieuwe auto, cadeaus voor de kleinkinderen én een droombruiloft in Afrika. In Zoetermeer weten ze wel raad met die gouden enveloppen. Gaston verrast 7 deelnemers op postcode 2729 ED met de PostcodeStraatprijs. 
 

vrijdag 11 september 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Videobellend met dochterlief 

Saskia videobelt met haar dochter als Gaston aanbelt. Als ze de cheque van € 25.000,- ziet, kan ze het bijna niet geloven. "Nee mijn god! Dit is bizar, hier kan ik zoveel mee!" Ze weet al waar een deel van haar prijs naartoe gaat. "Ik wil een andere auto kopen. Ik pas twee dagen per week op mijn kleinkind, dus die komt goed van pas." 

Dansend van geluk

Shudeska ligt nog in bed als Gaston aanbelt. Ze is druk aan het verbouwen en kan wel wat rust gebruiken. Maar als ze hoort dat ze € 25.000,- wint, is ze meteen klaarwakker. Ze danst met de cheque door de kamer! Naast haar verbouwing wil ze graag iets moois kopen voor haar kleinkinderen. 
 

Droombruiloft 

Ook Esdras en Monique krijgen geweldig nieuws: zij winnen € 50.000,-. Het stel is bijna 20 jaar getrouwd, maar heeft nog één grote wens. "We wilden heel graag in Afrika trouwen, maar dat is er toen niet van gekomen. Nu willen we die droom alsnog waarmaken voor ons 20-jarig jubileum!" En alsof dat nog niet genoeg is, winnen ze ook een BMW.

item.title: Spannende finale van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht Winnaarsverhalen 15 september 2026 Al twee jaar is René bezig met de verbouwing van zijn huis. Door zijn deelname aan de finale van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht komt het einde daarvan ineens een stuk sneller dichterbij. Lees meer
item.description:
Al twee jaar is René bezig met de verbouwing van zijn huis. Door zijn deelname aan de finale van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht komt het einde daarvan ineens een stuk sneller dichterbij. De 54-jarige timmerman uit Stad aan ’t Haringvliet bereikt de finale en gaat naar huis met maar liefst € 102.000,-.

dinsdag 15 september 2026 - Goede doelen

Een bijzondere koffer

René speelt de finale met koffer 8. Niet zomaar: zijn dochter Amber is op 8 december jarig. Vanuit de studio kijkt zijn vrouw Karin gespannen toe. Zij weet al precies wat ze met een eventuele geldprijs willen doen.

“René is al twee jaar aan het verbouwen. De buitenkant moet nog af, dus dat kunnen we dan laten doen”, vertelt ze.

“Ik ben met niets gekomen”

Met ‘Challenge King’ op zijn shirt speelt René dapper verder. De eerste drie biedingen van de bank blijven onder de € 100.000,-. Dan verschijnt er ineens een bod van maar liefst € 171.000,-.

Toch sluit de finalist het klepje. No deal. “Ik ben met niets gekomen”, zegt hij nuchter.

Het blijkt een moedige keuze. Kort daarna verdwijnt het hoogste bedrag van € 2,5 MILJOEN uit het spel. Wanneer de bank vervolgens € 102.000,- biedt, besluit René dat het genoeg is geweest. Hij drukt op de knop: deal!

Met de mooie geldprijs kunnen René en Karin hun huis eindelijk laten afmaken. En daarna? Dan is het tijd om samen van een heerlijke vakantie in Turkije te genieten.
item.content:encoded:
Al twee jaar is René bezig met de verbouwing van zijn huis. Door zijn deelname aan de finale van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht komt het einde daarvan ineens een stuk sneller dichterbij. De 54-jarige timmerman uit Stad aan ’t Haringvliet bereikt de finale en gaat naar huis met maar liefst € 102.000,-.

item.title: Our Common Purpose: Democratic Citizenship at America’s 250th Anniversary
item.description:
Photo by Michael DeStefano.

Danielle Allen, Stephen Heintz, and Eric Liu.

The following first appeared in Dædalus. The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily represent the views of the Rockefeller Brothers Fund.

In 2020, the American Academy of Arts & Sciences published Our Common Purpose, a vision for reinventing American democracy in the twenty-first century. The report set forth six strategies for strengthening institutions and civic fabric to create a virtuous cycle and reverse the vicious cycle of institutional dysfunction and weakened civic culture. 

The summer 2026 issue of Dædalus, the Academy's quarterly journal, surveys the efforts underway to renovate U.S. democracy six years after the report’s publication. 

This collection, guest edited by the cochairs of the Our Common Purpose commission Stephen Heintz, Danielle Allen, and Eric Liu, features fresh perspectives from scholars, civic leaders, and public servants on the current state and future of our democracy. The volume also includes responses by practitioners and advocates highlighting the greatest challenges they face—both locally and nationally—and the best approaches for overcoming them. 

As the essays in this issue make clear, in our era of rapid and profound transformation, looking backward will not suffice. In their introduction to the volume, Allen, Heintz, and Liu draw on Lincoln: “As our case is new, so we must think anew and act anew.”

As the United States marks its 250th anniversary this year, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences is not far behind. The Academy was founded in 1780, before the end of the Revolutionary War, by many of the same people who launched and prosecuted that war: John Hancock, George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, and others. John Adams was the first president of the Academy. These English subjects turned American revolutionaries recognized that they were embarking on something novel in the history of the world: establishing a self-governing society with the promise that its citizens would be free and equal. To advance this political experiment, they created the Academy, an organization to convene members of “the learned professions,” as those with professional expertise were called at the time. The charge assigned to this membership: “to cultivate every art and science which may tend to advance the interest, honor, dignity, and happiness of a free, independent, and virtuous people.”

It is important today to recognize what a leap of faith it was to create such an institution when the war was not yet won and the Revolution not yet secured. It is equally important to recognize the gap that existed even then between the new nation’s creed and its deeds.

The dilemma of slavery and its contradiction to the stated ideals of the founding were apparent to the founders of both the nation and the Academy. They recognized that this half-free, half-slave nation would have to innovate continuously, finding new ways of governing to help society navigate and negotiate the social and economic changes and crises that arise when there is a gap between our ideals and our institutions. They faced these realities with clear eyes and knew that this radical and flawed experiment in self-government would need to be capable of ceaseless adaptation and renovation.

In that spirit, the Academy has pursued projects to understand its own history and has also, in recent years, launched commissions to tackle the thorniest contemporary problems. This includes the Commission on the Practice of Democratic Citizenship, a group of thirty-five practitioners and scholars—diverse in professional expertise, geography, demographic background, and viewpoint—that we had the privilege to cochair starting in 2018. The Commission set out to answer the question of how we could improve American democratic self-government, with an emphasis on the centrality and agency of citizens, for the remainder of the twenty-­first century and beyond. In 2020, in a time of growing concern about the vitality and resilience of American democracy, the Commission published Our Common Purpose: Reinventing American Democracy for the 21st Century.

Our Common Purpose was shaped by the ethos of the Academy’s and our nation’s founders. We listened, learned, and deliberated. Notably, we achieved unanimity on thirty-one concrete recommendations for reinventing our democracy for the conditions of this century. And we worked with awareness of both the Academy’s strengths and weaknesses. We determined not to rely only on experts but to seek input from people in all walks of life. While we commissioned expert research as part of our foundational work for developing recommendations, we also conducted fifty listening sessions across the country in all kinds of communities: avid voters and people who had never voted; Naval Academy midshipmen and Cambodian refugees; Midwestern suburbanites and Angelenos of a range of political backgrounds. We asked people what they thought Americans shared, what their experience of our democracy was, and what the obstacles to their effective engagement were. We wanted to understand their frustrations, aspirations, and hopes.

We discovered the paradox that Americans have in common the feeling—amplified by media—that they have little in common. Yet we also found that people are hungering for connection, agency, and recognition. We learned that people find our political institutions nonresponsive and alienating. We heard a litany of challenges to participating in voting and in the civil society organizations of communities, from a disintegrating news environment to increasing polarization to opaque bureaucracy. We heard time and again that Americans feel they have little or no voice or power in our democratic institutions and processes. As such, they feel they have lost the ability to self-govern.

The central conceptual discovery of the work was offered by a listening session participant in Ellsworth, Maine. As he put it, in conversation, “A democratic society is a set of shared ideals, right? It only works as a group. That’s sort of its definition. And that, I think, can become a vicious circle. The worse the system’s working, the less effort people are going to put into the system.”

Here was a truth and plain recognition of our problem. We have been trapped in a vicious cycle: dysfunctional institutions diminish interest in participation; reduced engagement in civil society organizations means less learning and practice of the habits of compromise and negotiation; a weaker civic culture leads to worse decision-making inside our political institutions and concentrations of power in our society. And the cycle turns.

This diagnosis then made it possible for us to name the solution. We needed to flip the cycle from vicious to virtuous. In a healthy democracy, inclusive and responsive institutions motivate and facilitate participation; active participation in civic life cultivates and is sustained by a civic culture of mutual respect, willingness to compromise, collective problem-solving, and responsibility-taking; that vibrant civic culture, in turn, ensures that our institutions function well and remain responsive and adaptive to change.

But how can Americans flip the cycle from vicious to virtuous? There is no single way to do it. We realized that securing a healthy democracy to meet the profound challenges ahead in the remainder of the twenty-first century would require working to improve our political institutions, civil society infrastructure, and civic culture simultaneously. Our Commission set out to develop, vet, debate, and prioritize recommendations in all three domains.

We set ourselves a high bar for adopting recommendations. We are a cross-­ideological group, and we wanted every recommendation we developed to have support from both sides of the political spectrum. We would not require unanimity for any individual recommendation because we did not wish any single Commission member to have veto power. But we would reject any proposal that did not win support from both sides of the political spectrum. We took inspiration from Benjamin Franklin at the end of the Constitutional Convention: putting aside concerns he may have had with any particular article, Franklin offered support for the whole and urged the other delegates to do the same. The Commission acted in this spirit. We aimed for unanimous approval of a set of recommendations even if individual members of the Commission had reservations concerning one or another in particular.

This we achieved. Our cross-partisan Commission unanimously approved a set of thirty-one recommendations across strategies, addressing six imperatives:

  • to achieve equality of voice and representation through our political institutions;
  • to empower voters in a lasting way;
  • to ensure the responsiveness of our political institutions;
  • to dramatically expand the capacity of civil society organizations that foster “bridging” across lines of difference;
  • to build civic information architecture that supports common purpose; and
  • to inspire a culture of commitment to American constitutional democracy and one another.

The response to the report was galvanic. A diverse array of organizations became champions of Our Common Purpose, using it as a blueprint and a catalyst for action. Just as important, local leaders across the country raised their hands to become “OCP communities,” committing themselves to put our ideas into practice where they live. In short order, the Academy took a step with little precedent: it committed to a multiyear multimillion dollar initiative to make substantial progress on the implementation of these recommendations by the semiquincentennial in 2026.

We, our fellow Commission members, our broad network of champions, and the formidable Academy staff have for the past six years vigorously made the case for the strategies and recommendations intended to advance these imperatives. So how have we done? We can report remarkable advances across all six strategies, while also acknowledging that much work remains to be done.

Our collective efforts have inspired legislation, catalyzed public and private investment in civic life, and broadened support for the report’s theory of change and recommendations. Among our significant advances is the establishment of the Trust for Civic Life, a pooled fund and learning network to invest in local civic infrastructure in rural and small-town America. Other accomplishments include legislation introduced to increase the size of the House of Representatives, robust public discussion of establishing eighteen-year term limits for Supreme Court justices, bipartisan federal and state action to expand national service opportunities and funding, and the adoption of ranked-choice voting, automatic voter registration, and felon re-enfranchisement in several states and localities.

In 2021, a bipartisan group inspired by Our Common Purpose, the Educating for American Democracy initiative (EAD), released a roadmap for excellence in civics and history education. Twenty-eight states now have policy aligned with that roadmap; in thirty-nine states, schools and community learning partners like museums and historical societies are running EAD-aligned curricular or program pilots; and, by a conservative count, thousands of teachers and hundreds of thousands of students are engaged in EAD-aligned civic learning. National philanthropic endeavors like the New Pluralists Collaborative and place-based civic ventures like the Arizona Civic Life Partnership have embedded the concepts and narratives of Our Common Purpose into their work and strategies.

We also convened a working group of practitioners and scholars to more fully develop the concept of civic culture that was so central to the theory of action of our report. The result was Habits of Heart and Mind, an influential playbook on what civic culture is, why it matters, and how to fortify it. This was part of a series of blueprints for action developed by diverse expert working groups organized by the Academy. These working group reports addressed the following Commission recommendations:

  • Supreme Court justice term limits;
  • Expanding the House of Representatives;
  • Ranked-choice voting and multimember districts (proportional representation in the House of Representatives);
  • Establishing a Trust for Civic Life;
  • Fortifying civic culture; and
  • Preparing democratic citizens in higher education.

One more feature of our work deserves explicit mention. As noted above, the Constitution adopted in Philadelphia carried into the early life of our nation moral contestation over enslavement. Our social, political, and economic institutions entrenched racial domination. Successive generations of Americans have sought to rectify those original wrongs and build a true democracy for people of all backgrounds. In Our Common Purpose, we reviewed the history of the foundings and re-foundings of our nation: the original founding in 1776, the re-founding of Reconstruction, and another re-founding in the Civil Rights Movement. Even with the victories and triumphs achieved in each of these moments, it is also true that one after another generation of Americans has also failed to live up to our original founding aspirations. We have continually made our nation more perfect, but never perfect. Yet with each try we have fallen somewhat less short of our goals.

With our recommendations, we sought a fourth founding of the United States. Our age, too, has the responsibility to overcome fully the wrongs of racial domination and other forms of discrimination present in the original founding. We named this challenge as a central part of our diagnosis and wrote in our report: “Inequities continue to track lines of race, gender, and ethnicity, revealing deep structural unfairness in our society. A surge in white nationalism, anti-Semitism, and anti-immigrant vitriol has flooded our politics with sentiments corrosive to the ethic of a democratic society, while people of color continue to confront barriers to opportunity and participation.”

Our recommendations sought to address these challenges. Our strategy was novel and unfamiliar. It was not couched in an older language of procedural justice or color-blindness, nor in the now-common language of racial equity, racial justice, or antiracism. We focused on the question of how power is allocated and operates. In Our Common Purpose, we wrote:

The form of health needed by a constitutional democracy, even in times of crisis, flows from exactly the areas of focus in this report: equality of voice and representation, empowerment of voters, responsiveness of political institutions, bridging ties across lines of difference, civic information architecture that supports common purpose, and a culture of commitment to American constitutional democracy and one another.

Our conviction was that reforms to achieve equality of voice and representation through our political institutions; to empower voters in a lasting way; and to ensure the responsiveness of our political institutions would rebalance power and undo the long-lasting mechanisms of domination, whether racial, economic, or otherwise, that have characterized life throughout the history of our constitutional democracy.

We laid out a set of reforms designed to achieve a full sharing of civic power among all the members of this country’s incredibly heterogenous population. A particularly good example is the recommendation for the use of multimember districts, coupled with ranked-choice voting, for congressional elections. This voting methodology delivers emergent proportional representation, ensuring that the full spectrum of opinion in a district is represented in Congress and that minority perspectives are represented, regardless of whether those minorities are racial, cultural, or ideological. With the protections of the Voting Rights Act disassembled, this kind of reform provides an avenue for ensuring that power is fully shared across this nation’s diverse citizenry.

Now, as we observe the nation’s 250th anniversary, we have invited fresh perspectives on the future of our constitutional democracy. What should come next? For this volume, we have asked nine authors—many of them members of the Commission on the Practice of Democratic Citizenship—and sixteen respondents—practitioners and scholars with significant experience in these areas—to take up the strategies that we laid out in 2020 and to consider whether they remain fit for purpose. Where can we see progress? Where have we fallen short? How does each strategy matter for the future? Where should we put our energies and efforts? Should we prioritize any particular individual recommendations in the original report, or should we be turning our attention toward some new objectives? The collection is organized into six sections, each representing one of the report’s strategies.

Wallace Jefferson commends three institutional reforms in particular as worthy of continued effort: increasing the size of the House of Representatives, achieving term limits for Supreme Court justices, and spreading the use of ranked-choice voting.

Lisa García Bedolla evaluates our recommendations of reforms to empower voters and finds that—while they put the right incentives in place—they will not significantly drive the inclusion of those currently left out unless supplemented by robust work on civic culture and practices of inviting people into participation.

Carolyn Lukensmeyer surveys the rapidly burgeoning field of democratic deliberation and citizens’ assemblies—conducted in both analog and digital forms—and finds that this new institutional design is finally taking flight within the institutions of American representative democracy. She considers this a success and urges further effort in this direction.

Ethan Zuckerman offers a bleak assessment of the state of journalism and social media and underscores how far away we still are from having the research access that we need into the operations of social media platforms. There has been productive experimentation with decentralized forms of technology, but the balance of power still resides very much with the closed and opaque industry titans.

David Campbell celebrates the growing civic education movement and argues that it requires sharper focus on one civic skill in particular: how to disagree better.

On expanding civic bridging capacity, Charlie Brown and Christina Jodice outline the Trust for Civic Life’s mission and progress in deploying $50 million across communities in rural America; Daniel Stid highlights the Trust as a breakthrough for democracy-related philanthropy and suggests how national foundations broadly can innovate and reorient funding patterns to support associational life; and Kristen Bennett looks toward national service as a means to connect across lines of difference and foster democratic participation.

Taken together, the reflections, ideas, and responses in this volume form a composite picture of the state of the democracy-renovation movement today. The institutional and civic culture work that Our Common Purpose catalyzed has coalesced into a well-understood and widely affirmed agenda. The champions and allies we activated have gained ground on some parts of the agenda and have faced setbacks on others, and their efforts continue.

The 250th anniversary is an appropriate time to celebrate our achievements as a nation, to identify our shortcomings forthrightly, and to imagine how to advance the aspirations embedded in the ethos and ideals of 1776—the “electric cord” of the commitment to human equality, as Lincoln called it. At the same time, we are also in an era of rapid transformation; looking backward will not suffice. We can learn from Lincoln here too: “As our case is new, so we must think anew and act anew.”

This next phase of work requires us to integrate the powers of AI into this agenda for democracy renovation. How can we put powerful new agentic technologies to work to help us solve the problems of representation, participation, civil society engagement, media, and civic education? Of course, AI tools will also bring further challenges for democracy, and so our work on governance must equip our constitutional democracy also to govern AI. Successful governance through such rapid social and economic transformation requires civic strength cultivated through a renewal of our civic culture, and responsive, agile governance achieved through renovation of our political institutions.

In addition, we must focus more on the relationship between economic conditions and the vitality of democracy, between economic and political inequality. In recognition of the problems with the nation’s political economy, the Commission recommended in 2020 that the Academy organize a separate group to examine the economic realities of Americans and offer recommendations to improve their economic well-being. That body, the Commission on Reimagining Our Economy (CORE), issued its report, Advancing a People-First Economy, and a companion photo­journal, Faces of America, in fall 2023.

But there is more to do, and these issues have only grown more urgent in the years since CORE released its recommendations. The rise of an AI-dominated economy threatens to undermine the promise of shared prosperityand our fundamental humanity. The continued concentration of political power in the federal executive and economic clout in a tiny oligarchic elite runs counter to both conservative principles of decentralized power and progressive principles of justice. What will it take now to make our economy more democratic and more committed to individual flourishing? What will it take to reduce the distorting effect of hyper-concentrated wealth on our democracy? How can we fortify a cross-ideological commitment to the local, to the role of place and relationship in making both our economy and polity more inclusive? These are questions the Academy is taking on in new initiatives inspired by the precedents of Our Common Purpose and CORE.

Though the Commission on the Practice of Democratic Citizenship has concluded its six-year mission to change the frame of the possible in democracy renovation, we three cochairs and our flotilla of affiliated organizations and allies remain dedicated to its purposes. We expect to stay at this work through at least the 250th anniversary of the Bill of Rights, in 2041. If we and our fellow champions can bring the same clarity of focus, creativity, energy, and goodwill to this work for the coming fifteen years, we believe a fourth founding of the United States will indeed unfold.

As you read the essays in this volume, we hope you will keep active in your minds the image of the cycle that is either virtuous or vicious, in which our political institutions, civic culture, and civil society influence each other. Then keep active in your hearts the sense of responsibility for pushing that cycle in the direction that advances the “interest, honor, dignity, and happiness of a free, independent, and virtuous people.” That is the spirit of Our Common Purpose, of the American Academy, and of the experiment in constitutional democracy that all Americans have the blessing and the burden to steward and reinvent.

Read the full collection of essays in the summer 2026 issue of Dædalus.

  • Preparing democratic citizens in higher education.

One more feature of our work deserves explicit mention. As noted above, the Constitution adopted in Philadelphia carried into the early life of our nation moral contestation over enslavement. Our social, political, and economic institutions entrenched racial domination. Successive generations of Americans have sought to rectify those original wrongs and build a true democracy for people of all backgrounds. In Our Common Purpose, we reviewed the history of the foundings and re-foundings of our nation: the original founding in 1776, the re-founding of Reconstruction, and another re-founding in the Civil Rights Movement. Even with the victories and triumphs achieved in each of these moments, it is also true that one after another generation of Americans has also failed to live up to our original founding aspirations. We have continually made our nation more perfect, but never perfect. Yet with each try we have fallen somewhat less short of our goals.

With our recommendations, we sought a fourth founding of the United States. Our age, too, has the responsibility to overcome fully the wrongs of racial domination and other forms of discrimination present in the original founding. We named this challenge as a central part of our diagnosis and wrote in our report: “Inequities continue to track lines of race, gender, and ethnicity, revealing deep structural unfairness in our society. A surge in white nationalism, anti-Semitism, and anti-immigrant vitriol has flooded our politics with sentiments corrosive to the ethic of a democratic society, while people of color continue to confront barriers to opportunity and participation.”

Our recommendations sought to address these challenges. Our strategy was novel and unfamiliar. It was not couched in an older language of procedural justice or color-blindness, nor in the now-common language of racial equity, racial justice, or antiracism. We focused on the question of how power is allocated and operates. In Our Common Purpose, we wrote:

The form of health needed by a constitutional democracy, even in times of crisis, flows from exactly the areas of focus in this report: equality of voice and representation, empowerment of voters, responsiveness of political institutions, bridging ties across lines of difference, civic information architecture that supports common purpose, and a culture of commitment to American constitutional democracy and one another.

Our conviction was that reforms to achieve equality of voice and representation through our political institutions; to empower voters in a lasting way; and to ensure the responsiveness of our political institutions would rebalance power and undo the long-lasting mechanisms of domination, whether racial, economic, or otherwise, that have characterized life throughout the history of our constitutional democracy.

We laid out a set of reforms designed to achieve a full sharing of civic power among all the members of this country’s incredibly heterogenous population. A particularly good example is the recommendation for the use of multimember districts, coupled with ranked-choice voting, for congressional elections. This voting methodology delivers emergent proportional representation, ensuring that the full spectrum of opinion in a district is represented in Congress and that minority perspectives are represented, regardless of whether those minorities are racial, cultural, or ideological. With the protections of the Voting Rights Act disassembled, this kind of reform provides an avenue for ensuring that power is fully shared across this nation’s diverse citizenry.

Now, as we observe the nation’s 250th anniversary, we have invited fresh perspectives on the future of our constitutional democracy. What should come next? For this volume, we have asked nine authors—many of them members of the Commission on the Practice of Democratic Citizenship—and sixteen respondents—practitioners and scholars with significant experience in these areas—to take up the strategies that we laid out in 2020 and to consider whether they remain fit for purpose. Where can we see progress? Where have we fallen short? How does each strategy matter for the future? Where should we put our energies and efforts? Should we prioritize any particular individual recommendations in the original report, or should we be turning our attention toward some new objectives? The collection is organized into six sections, each representing one of the report’s strategies.

Wallace Jefferson commends three institutional reforms in particular as worthy of continued effort: increasing the size of the House of Representatives, achieving term limits for Supreme Court justices, and spreading the use of ranked-choice voting.

Lisa García Bedolla evaluates our recommendations of reforms to empower voters and finds that—while they put the right incentives in place—they will not significantly drive the inclusion of those currently left out unless supplemented by robust work on civic culture and practices of inviting people into participation.

Carolyn Lukensmeyer surveys the rapidly burgeoning field of democratic deliberation and citizens’ assemblies—conducted in both analog and digital forms—and finds that this new institutional design is finally taking flight within the institutions of American representative democracy. She considers this a success and urges further effort in this direction.

Ethan Zuckerman offers a bleak assessment of the state of journalism and social media and underscores how far away we still are from having the research access that we need into the operations of social media platforms. There has been productive experimentation with decentralized forms of technology, but the balance of power still resides very much with the closed and opaque industry titans.

David Campbell celebrates the growing civic education movement and argues that it requires sharper focus on one civic skill in particular: how to disagree better.

On expanding civic bridging capacity, Charlie Brown and Christina Jodice outline the Trust for Civic Life’s mission and progress in deploying $50 million across communities in rural America; Daniel Stid highlights the Trust as a breakthrough for democracy-related philanthropy and suggests how national foundations broadly can innovate and reorient funding patterns to support associational life; and Kristen Bennett looks toward national service as a means to connect across lines of difference and foster democratic participation.

Taken together, the reflections, ideas, and responses in this volume form a composite picture of the state of the democracy-renovation movement today. The institutional and civic culture work that Our Common Purpose catalyzed has coalesced into a well-understood and widely affirmed agenda. The champions and allies we activated have gained ground on some parts of the agenda and have faced setbacks on others, and their efforts continue.

The 250th anniversary is an appropriate time to celebrate our achievements as a nation, to identify our shortcomings forthrightly, and to imagine how to advance the aspirations embedded in the ethos and ideals of 1776—the “electric cord” of the commitment to human equality, as Lincoln called it. At the same time, we are also in an era of rapid transformation; looking backward will not suffice. We can learn from Lincoln here too: “As our case is new, so we must think anew and act anew.”

This next phase of work requires us to integrate the powers of AI into this agenda for democracy renovation. How can we put powerful new agentic technologies to work to help us solve the problems of representation, participation, civil society engagement, media, and civic education? Of course, AI tools will also bring further challenges for democracy, and so our work on governance must equip our constitutional democracy also to govern AI. Successful governance through such rapid social and economic transformation requires civic strength cultivated through a renewal of our civic culture, and responsive, agile governance achieved through renovation of our political institutions.

In addition, we must focus more on the relationship between economic conditions and the vitality of democracy, between economic and political inequality. In recognition of the problems with the nation’s political economy, the Commission recommended in 2020 that the Academy organize a separate group to examine the economic realities of Americans and offer recommendations to improve their economic well-being. That body, the Commission on Reimagining Our Economy (CORE), issued its report, Advancing a People-First Economy, and a companion photo­journal, Faces of America, in fall 2023.

But there is more to do, and these issues have only grown more urgent in the years since CORE released its recommendations. The rise of an AI-dominated economy threatens to undermine the promise of shared prosperityand our fundamental humanity. The continued concentration of political power in the federal executive and economic clout in a tiny oligarchic elite runs counter to both conservative principles of decentralized power and progressive principles of justice. What will it take now to make our economy more democratic and more committed to individual flourishing? What will it take to reduce the distorting effect of hyper-concentrated wealth on our democracy? How can we fortify a cross-ideological commitment to the local, to the role of place and relationship in making both our economy and polity more inclusive? These are questions the Academy is taking on in new initiatives inspired by the precedents of Our Common Purpose and CORE.

Though the Commission on the Practice of Democratic Citizenship has concluded its six-year mission to change the frame of the possible in democracy renovation, we three cochairs and our flotilla of affiliated organizations and allies remain dedicated to its purposes. We expect to stay at this work through at least the 250th anniversary of the Bill of Rights, in 2041. If we and our fellow champions can bring the same clarity of focus, creativity, energy, and goodwill to this work for the coming fifteen years, we believe a fourth founding of the United States will indeed unfold.

As you read the essays in this volume, we hope you will keep active in your minds the image of the cycle that is either virtuous or vicious, in which our political institutions, civic culture, and civil society influence each other. Then keep active in your hearts the sense of responsibility for pushing that cycle in the direction that advances the “interest, honor, dignity, and happiness of a free, independent, and virtuous people.” That is the spirit of Our Common Purpose, of the American Academy, and of the experiment in constitutional democracy that all Americans have the blessing and the burden to steward and reinvent.

Read the full collection of essays in the summer 2026 issue of Dædalus.

item.title: A Deeper Look at How SmartStart Creates Educational and Economic Opportunity for South Africans
item.description:
The power of seeing potential where others see only challenge

Sometimes, the most powerful innovation doesn’t come from building something new, but from seeing existing assets in a new light.

In South Africa, families and governments faced a dilemma: nearly one-third of three- to five-year-olds lacked access to high-quality early education that could transform the trajectory of their lives, yet the traditional solution—capital-intensive formal learning centers—are unrealistic in the communities that need them most.

So, what to do?

Under the leadership of Founding CEO Grace Matlhape, 2026 Skoll Awardee SmartStart designed a model to leverage existing community assets to tackle the problem. Low-income communities have plenty of physical spaces, such as homes and community centers, and they’re bursting with local talent and capacity.

In recognition of these opportunities, SmartStart equipped thousands of community members, most of whom are women, to operate early learning centers out of their homes and similar spaces—closing the learning achievement gap for children while, at the same time, creating dignified, high-quality careers in areas plagued by high unemployment.

Here’s how they did it:

What sets the innovation apart is the organization’s so-called social franchise model, in which SmartStart provides training, materials, coaching, compliance support, and peer networks to franchisees via a single platform. This approach addresses two persistent challenges simultaneously: affordability of care, and economic instability for communities. It’s an elegant solution that is easily scalable nationwide.

In some of South Africa’s informal settlements and marginalized townships, jobless rates can climb as high as 60–70 percent, and young children who live there are undercounted and overlooked. These families simply fall through the cracks.

Yet the national government has declared a goal of ensuring universal early education access by 2030. SmartStart’s social franchise model is an affordable way to achieve that stated ambition.

“We have to solve for those children,” Matlhape says. “It isn’t possible to wish there was a piece of land where you could build a center. …You have to work with what you have.”

How the model delivers lasting, scalable change

The SmartStart team is vocal about their role in a broader ecosystem of actors engaged in collective action to create lasting change within South Africa’s educational and economic systems. The organization’s deep partnership with the government is paramount to the viability of the model. They’ve worked together to shift attitudes about what quality early education programs can look like, amend regulations to support home-based learning, and collaborate on shared goals related to increasing access.

After establishing program delivery infrastructure in all nine South African provinces—reaching more than 160,000 children every week—SmartStart is now focusing on building broader partnerships to enable even more access, including implementing systems, advocating for policies, and disseminating lessons to support continued expansion of early learning. These steps are extending the organization’s impact far beyond its delivery footprint.

But success is not all about growth, infrastructure, and systems. SmartStart underscores the importance of a heart-led approach when working with children; it’s an ingredient as essential as the robust curriculum.

All practitioners in the SmartStart network emphasize three things: love, play, and talk. These values are elevated not only because it’s the right thing to do, Matlhape said, but also because it garners “the outcomes we’re looking for.”

And it’s working. Children in SmartStart’s programs demonstrate significant improvements in math, literacy, and fine motor skills. The percentage of children who are “on track” across five developmental domains increased from 45 percent to 65 percent in just eight months, while the proportion of children “falling far behind” was nearly halved.

Ultimately, children who receive high-quality early education are better prepared for formal schooling, are more likely to complete secondary education, and are more likely to secure meaningful and financially stable careers as adults.

Beyond children, the ripple effects of SmartStart’s program on communities’ economic development are profound. In addition to gaining greater financial security for themselves, early learning practitioners often employ several additional community members. And, with their children in reliable care, parents are able to focus on their own livelihoods.

Learn more about how SmartStart is creating opportunity across generations of South Africans.

The post A Deeper Look at How SmartStart Creates Educational and Economic Opportunity for South Africans appeared first on Skoll.org.

item.title: Een stukje geluk op postcode 4053 HM Winnaarsverhalen 11 september 2026 De zon schijnt volop in IJzendoorn als Gaston de winnaars op postcode 4053 HM verrast met de PostcodeStraatprijs. Lees meer
item.description:
De zon schijnt volop in IJzendoorn als Gaston de winnaars op postcode 4053 HM verrast met de PostcodeStraatprijs. Zodra de gouden enveloppen opengaan, verschijnen grote glimlachen én de eerste tranen. Van een trip naar Texel tot nieuwe meubels: de plannen komen al snel op tafel. En voor Ellen krijgt de middag nog een extra feestelijk tintje. 

vrijdag 11 september 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Op naar Texel 

Michiel en Margret hebben samen een zaak in het dorp. Hij is kapper en zij werkt als pedicure. Over hun plannen met de € 25.000,- hoeven ze niet lang na te denken. "We willen graag naar Texel toe."

Een stukje geluk

Met ‘Challenge King’ op zijn shirt speelt René dapper verder. De eerste drie biedingen van de bank blijven onder de € 100.000,-. Dan verschijnt er ineens een bod van maar liefst € 171.000,-.

Ook Bert is zichtbaar blij met zijn cheque van € 25.000,-. "Je bent elke week welkom. Dit is een stukje geluk", zegt hij tegen Gaston. Een bestemming voor het geld heeft hij ook al. Een aantal meubels is aan vervanging toe. Daar komt deze prijs dus mooi voor van pas.

Mooie reisjes met de viervoeter 

Voor Ellen blijft het niet bij € 25.000,-. Gaston heeft nóg een verrassing voor haar. Als hij de sleutels van een gloednieuwe BMW tevoorschijn haalt, schieten de tranen in haar ogen. Al snel wordt er gefantaseerd over de mooie ritten die ze samen met haar hond en haar nieuwe auto kan maken. Wat een middag!

item.title: Resto van harte 20 jarig jubileum Goede doelen 10 september 2026 Anderhalf jaar geleden ging Marcel met pensioen. Hij zocht een leuke activiteit en wilde graag nieuwe mensen uit zijn buurt leren kennen. Lees meer
item.description:
Anderhalf jaar geleden ging Marcel met pensioen. Hij zocht een leuke activiteit en wilde graag nieuwe mensen uit zijn buurt leren kennen. Tijdens het uitlaten van zijn hond raakte hij aan de praat met een paar buurtgenoten. Zij vertelden enthousiast over Resto VanHarte. Marcel besloot een keer mee te gaan. Inmiddels schuift hij iedere dinsdagavond aan bij Resto VanHarte in Amsterdam Zuidoost Holendrecht. “Ik wil geen avond missen, want het is echt een feestje.” 

donderdag 10 september 2026 - Goede doelen

Meteen onderdeel van de familie 

Vanaf zijn eerste bezoek voelt Marcel zich welkom. “De koks, vrijwilligers en gasten zijn allemaal even persoonlijk en warm. Ik was gelijk onderdeel van de familie.” 

Die gezelligheid blijft niet aan tafel. Marcel komt regelmatig andere gasten tegen in de buurt. “Dan hebben we elkaar meteen wat te vertellen. Zo voel ik me nog meer verbonden met de buurt.” 

Dat is precies wat samen eten kan doen. Je deelt niet alleen een maaltijd, maar ook verhalen en mooie momenten. Zo ontstaan nieuwe contacten. En soms zelfs vriendschappen. 

Een avond vol aandacht 

Bij Resto VanHarte draait het daarom om meer dan lekker eten. Vrijwilligers zorgen voor een warm welkom en een fijne sfeer. 

Dat merkt Marcel iedere week. “Een van de vrijwilligers heet ons altijd welkom met een praatje en neemt het menu door. Zijn vrouw speelt vaak een stuk piano voor ons. En laatst had een vrijwilliger van het buurthuis heerlijke Surinaamse bara’s meegenomen. Het is echt genieten.” 

Resto VanHarte organiseert dit soort diners op veel plekken in Nederland. Iedereen is welkom. Zo brengt de organisatie buurtbewoners bij elkaar en helpt ze eenzaamheid te verminderen. Mede dankzij de deelnemers van de Postcode Loterij kan Resto VanHarte in steeds meer buurten mensen samenbrengen.

Resto VanHarte organiseert dit soort diners op veel plekken in Nederland. Iedereen is welkom. Zo brengt de organisatie buurtbewoners bij elkaar en helpt ze eenzaamheid te verminderen. Mede dankzij de deelnemers van de Postcode Loterij kan Resto VanHarte in steeds meer buurten mensen samenbrengen.

item.title: NewsStudy reveals only 30% of South African Publishers Block AI Crawlers despite widespread fair use concerns A new study, Protocol Gap: South Africa, reveals that only a third of publishers in South Africa are actively aiming to limit AI crawler access to their content using robots.txt; these are files that allow a site owner to tell search engine crawlers which URLs they can access on the site, and which ones they should avoid. The new data from South Africa reveals that these AI-blocking measures are concentrated among larger and better-resourced publishers while smaller outlets remain widely exposed to scraping – the same outlets whose sustainability is most at risk due to declining traffic and referrals.
item.description:
Press Releases

A new study, Protocol Gap: South Africa, reveals that only a third of publishers in South Africa are actively aiming to limit AI crawler access to their content using robots.txt; these are files that allow a site owner to tell search engine crawlers which URLs they can access on the site, and which ones they should avoid. The new data from South Africa reveals that these AI-blocking measures are concentrated among larger and better-resourced publishers while smaller outlets remain widely exposed to scraping – the same outlets whose sustainability is most at risk due to declining traffic and referrals.

Over the last year, South Africa’s leading news sites have lost an average of 20% of their daily page views, mirroring international dynamics. As extraction and use of publisher content by AI companies increases, often without compensation or attribution, it accelerates visibility issues that threaten the survival of newsrooms – in South Africa and beyond.

In late 2025, the South African Competition Commission concluded a landmark Media and Digital Platforms Market Inquiry (MDPMI), which found that publishers are increasingly being forced to make trade-offs between maintaining visibility and protecting their content.  In this context, use of robots.txt is one indicator of how publishers are responding to growing pressure to decide whether and how their content can be accessed by automated crawlers. The Protocol Gap report’s findings contribute to ongoing debates in South Africa’s media sector on application of competition law, copyright reform, and the development of a national AI policy framework.

Robots.txt is a text file that can be added to the root domain of a website that contains instructions to search engines and web crawlers about what content they can access. This includes directives to AI bots that systematically browse and collect data to train LLMs and power AI assistants and search engines. Robots.txt is one of the few free tools available to content creators to signal how they want their data to be used by AI companies. While not legally binding, robots.txt has been used in legal complaints against unauthorised crawling and scraping in Canada, US, and UK. The file can serve as leverage in licensing negotiations, especially where AI models rely heavily on large volumes of unconsented, uncompensated data. However, effectiveness depends on voluntary compliance by AI developers, and its role within broader governance frameworks remains contested.

Based on analysis of 263 news websites, Protocol Gap: South Africa finds that while 74.1% of publishers have a robots.txt file in place, only 30.4% block at least one AI crawler as of April 2026. Although the percentage of publishers that use robots.txt to block AI crawlers rose modestly from 29.7% in December 2025 to 30.4%, the findings suggest that most publishers remain open to AI data collection.

Below these broad findings, the study identified a gap in adoption of AI-scraping policies between large and small publishers that reflects disparities in resources, technical capacity, referral traffic dependency, and strategic positioning. This raises important questions about bargaining power, content ownership and sustainability, as AI systems become increasingly reliant on news content. In the absence of clear legal and regulatory frameworks, the decisions publishers make now about how AI crawlers access their content could have long-lasting consequences.

The report, released by the Media Leadership Think Tank (MLTT) at the GIBS Business School (Gordon Institute of Business Science), the Journalism Relay Project, and the International Fund for Public Interest Media (IFPIM) is part of a broader research collaboration focused on Brazil, Indonesia, and South Africa. Through technical and qualitative research, it aims to increase awareness among media organizations on how AI systems access their content and help to inform strategies and policies to manage AI crawlers in ways that best serve newsroom interests. The report includes a detailed methodology for all those who may want to replicate this research on robots.txt in other countries and regions.

The study also provides a replicable methodology for researchers and publisher associations interested in conducting similar audits and concludes with next steps for research and engagement with ongoing efforts to strengthen publisher agency, bargaining power, and transparency in emerging AI licensing ecosystems.

‍

Full suite of Protocol Gap reports: ctrl-j.info/publications

‍

item.title: StoryIn a country under fire, a radio station refuses to let the signal go darkHromadske Radio, one of Ukraine's few independent, non-commercial and non-governmental news and talk radio stations, is among the outlets that have come under attack by Russian forces. Since 2022, nine of its transmitters have been destroyed or seized. It has continued to broadcast anyway, 24/7 across seven FM transmitters, five of them in frontline regions.
item.description:
Press Releases

Paris, 20 August: In Ukraine, reliable information can be a matter of survival, especially for those living on the frontlines. Yet since Russia's full-scale invasion, journalists and the infrastructure they depend on have been deliberately targeted, making the reporting of attacks, troop movements, aid deliveries and reconstruction an immensely dangerous job.

Hromadske Radio, one of Ukraine's few independent, non-commercial and non-governmental news and talk radio stations, is among the outlets that have come under attack. Since 2022, nine of its transmitters have been destroyed or seized by Russian troops.  It has continued to broadcast anyway, 24/7 across seven FM transmitters, five of them in frontline regions.  Their radio broadcasts are particularly meaningful for those on the contact line: when drone strikes take out the power grid, hand-held, battery-powered radios are one of the only channels for audiences in occupied and combat zones to get factual, up-to-date information, much of it essential to their safety and support needs.

Hromadske Radio relayed to IFPIM staff that when Russian shelling has disrupted their ability to broadcast on the frontlines, they have received constant messages from residents hoping for news to be restored.

“Two women from the "red zone" of Kherson called. I spoke with them and you could hear the shelling even over the phone. They complained that they can't hear Hromadske Radio, because they used to wake up and fall asleep with us,” said Ruslana Brianska, Executive Director of Hromadske Radio. “One woman is blind, she is 81, and she said she wants to support us financially — for her that's very important... She sent greetings to everyone. She knows us all by our voices and especially always waits for the 5:00 PM news bulletin.” Messages like these inspire the station’s tireless effort to maintain and expand broadcasting.

Like many markets, Ukraine was hit hard by the closure of USAID, which had supported independent, public interest media as a pillar of democracy. Some 333 outlets have shut down in the country over the past four years, lost to a combination of collapsing ad revenue and aid cuts. In 2024, the International Fund awarded flexible funding to Hromadske Radio to sustain its delivery of trustworthy news to audiences in Ukraine and the diaspora. The Fund's grant has helped Hromadske Radio expand its digital presence, build a coherent brand strategy, diversify its income and, most of all, keep broadcasting despite the challenging security situation.

"When a station like Hromadske Radio stays on air through bombardment and blackout, it's not just reporting the war, it's holding a society together.”

"When a station like Hromadske Radio stays on air through bombardment and blackout, it's not just reporting the war, it's holding a society together,” said Rita Rudusa, IFPIM’s Regional Director for Eastern Europe. “Independent media is one of the first things authoritarian forces try to destroy, and one of the last things the world remembers to fund. Our role is to make sure outlets like this can stay the course during the war, and survive beyond it."

Hromadske Radio’s experience is representative of the challenges facing Ukrainian news media more broadly. According to Reporters Without Borders (RSF) more than 175 Ukrainian and international journalists have been victims of Russian attacks in the four years since the invasion began. That figure includes 16 killed, at least 56 injured—mostly in drone strikes—and 26 detained. Beyond attacks on individuals, RSF has documented at least 25 attacks on news infrastructure, like those sustained by Hromadske Radio, including the bombing and occupation of broadcasting towers. In occupied regions, Russian forces routinely move to cut off Ukrainian programming and replace it with pro-Russia radio content and misleading narratives. In this context, direct support to independent outlets can be a gamechanger when it comes to ensuring the continued presence of a free and independent press.  

“We must keep the transmitters in frontline regions running: these are investments that determine whether or not people there hear verified information,” said Viktoriia Yermolaieva, Editor in Chief of Hromadske Radio. “In this context, core funding allows us to maintain our capacity to operate, keep the team together, invest in rapidly developing technologies, improve our format, increase the quantity and quality of content, pay for critically important infrastructure, and continue broadcasting where people urgently need it. This gives Hromadske Radio not just funding for an individual project, but stability—the ability to plan, develop, and set editorial priorities according to the needs of the audience and life in wartime conditions.”

By being able to stay and deliver, Hromadske Radio is now a trusted news source for roughly 580,000 weekly listeners. Their reach on YouTube and Facebook both has increased by ~65% since they became an IFPIM grantee, meaningful growth for an organization with mature social channels. In addition to reaching people on radio waves and digital channels, Hromadske Radio has started hosting in-person events designed to translate the subjects of their reporting into live dialogues. The events covered social topics like gender equality, LGBTQ+ rights, Ukrainian-Jewish history, and media accountability. The station has also invested heavily in making their website and programs accessible for those with disabilities—implementing AI powered voiceovers for all articles and alt text for images—and helping other newsrooms do the same. For this work, the station received an award for ‘Best Practices for Equality and Diversity in Ukrainian Newsrooms,’ in March 2026 from the National Council of Ukraine for Television and Radio Broadcasting, a national "Women in Media" NGO, and International Media Support.

Especially during a war, where information is contested as fiercely as territory, independent journalism is not a luxury. It is infrastructure, as vital as power lines or roads, and just as hard to rebuild once lost. Supporting outlets like Hromadske Radio is how democratic governments and others opposed to autocracy can ensure that news infrastructure remains where it is needed most, and that reliable facts and information can reach people in even the darkest conditions.

‍

item.title: A Deeper Look at How Indus Action Helps Strengthen India’s Social and Economic Safety Net
item.description:
How a model built on trust brings social and financial benefits within reach for more vulnerable families 

How do you support workers and their families in a country where there is no shared definition of “work”?  

Nine in 10 working citizens in India are employed in the informal sector—often in daily gigs that lack income stability. This intense job insecurity in a country with some 600 million people of working age is one of the challenges Indus Action sought to address. 

The organization, a 2026 Skoll Awardee, fills the gap between government intent and real-world impact. It helps millions of Indians understand, access, and claim benefits from more than 5,000 social protection programs the government offers, targeting workers, students, new mothers, and others experiencing life shocks.

India’s benefits programs are generous, but they’re also complex, difficult to understand, and require onerous application processes. As such, they’re functionally inaccessible for many of the people they are intended to support.

Indus Action’s technological, mobile-first solutions and community outreach are particularly welcome for the diverse population of informal workers who aren’t aware of the labor protections available to them. Even those who know they are eligible often don’t have the time, know-how, or flexibility in their daily schedules to carry out the average of 10 steps needed to claim benefits.

But the cost of not doing so is incredibly high:

By building the government’s capacity to deliver entitlement programs, strengthening community outreach, and harnessing technology to design and roll out citizen-centric solutions, Indus Action has connected 3.4 million citizens with their entitlements. This includes 1.8 million workers who received livelihood benefits.

On a macro level, Indus Action’s ability to help the government scale its intended labor protections for workers ultimately has the potential to create clearer pathways toward greater economic mobility for millions. The impact is particularly stark in the construction sector, which, as India’s second-largest industry, employs 71 million people and is projected to top 100 million by 2030.

Yet this sector is particularly vulnerable to economic shocks due to temporary work arrangements, informal relationships with employers, and frequent relocations to new job sites. These barriers make it difficult to demonstrate eligibility for existing welfare programs.

And with a growing Indian population that relies on functional infrastructure such as roads and airports, construction is vital to the country’s economic growth—highlighting that Indus Action’s support for this population is a positive force for greater economic stability overall.

In addition to workers, Indus Action helps families navigate what it calls “moments that matter,” such as the birth of a child, a period of unemployment, claiming a pension, or earning a scholarship. It has helped 949,842 students access school admissions or scholarships and more than 172,446 mothers access maternity health benefits. Together, these benefits help millions of people chart pathways out of poverty—lifting the entire economy.

What Makes the Model Successful

Founder and CEO Tarun Cherukuri emphasizes the importance of building two-way trust between citizens and government, including the last-mile community outreach workers responsible for registering individuals for benefits. His vision for Indus Action is to infuse greater relationship-building into a system that can often feel faceless.

“That’s our societal vision: this idea of relational state capacity,” he says, “where both sides—the citizen and the last-mile worker—are able to see each other’s humanity.”

Learn more about Indus Action’s impact on families.

The post A Deeper Look at How Indus Action Helps Strengthen India’s Social and Economic Safety Net appeared first on Skoll.org.

How a model built on trust brings social and financial benefits within reach for more vulnerable families 

How do you support workers and their families in a country where there is no shared definition of “work”?  

Nine in 10 working citizens in India are employed in the informal sector—often in daily gigs that lack income stability. This intense job insecurity in a country with some 600 million people of working age is one of the challenges Indus Action sought to address. 

The organization, a 2026 Skoll Awardee, fills the gap between government intent and real-world impact. It helps millions of Indians understand, access, and claim benefits from more than 5,000 social protection programs the government offers, targeting workers, students, new mothers, and others experiencing life shocks.

India’s benefits programs are generous, but they’re also complex, difficult to understand, and require onerous application processes. As such, they’re functionally inaccessible for many of the people they are intended to support.

Indus Action’s technological, mobile-first solutions and community outreach are particularly welcome for the diverse population of informal workers who aren’t aware of the labor protections available to them. Even those who know they are eligible often don’t have the time, know-how, or flexibility in their daily schedules to carry out the average of 10 steps needed to claim benefits.

But the cost of not doing so is incredibly high:

By building the government’s capacity to deliver entitlement programs, strengthening community outreach, and harnessing technology to design and roll out citizen-centric solutions, Indus Action has connected 3.4 million citizens with their entitlements. This includes 1.8 million workers who received livelihood benefits.

On a macro level, Indus Action’s ability to help the government scale its intended labor protections for workers ultimately has the potential to create clearer pathways toward greater economic mobility for millions. The impact is particularly stark in the construction sector, which, as India’s second-largest industry, employs 71 million people and is projected to top 100 million by 2030.

Yet this sector is particularly vulnerable to economic shocks due to temporary work arrangements, informal relationships with employers, and frequent relocations to new job sites. These barriers make it difficult to demonstrate eligibility for existing welfare programs.

And with a growing Indian population that relies on functional infrastructure such as roads and airports, construction is vital to the country’s economic growth—highlighting that Indus Action’s support for this population is a positive force for greater economic stability overall.

In addition to workers, Indus Action helps families navigate what it calls “moments that matter,” such as the birth of a child, a period of unemployment, claiming a pension, or earning a scholarship. It has helped 949,842 students access school admissions or scholarships and more than 172,446 mothers access maternity health benefits. Together, these benefits help millions of people chart pathways out of poverty—lifting the entire economy.

What Makes the Model Successful

Founder and CEO Tarun Cherukuri emphasizes the importance of building two-way trust between citizens and government, including the last-mile community outreach workers responsible for registering individuals for benefits. His vision for Indus Action is to infuse greater relationship-building into a system that can often feel faceless.

“That’s our societal vision: this idea of relational state capacity,” he says, “where both sides—the citizen and the last-mile worker—are able to see each other’s humanity.”

Learn more about Indus Action’s impact on families.

The post A Deeper Look at How Indus Action Helps Strengthen India’s Social and Economic Safety Net appeared first on Skoll.org.
